analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set federal discharge limits on PFAS 'forever chemicals' from eight polluting industries.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2025 with one cosponsor, the bill has sat in a House subcommittee since February 2026 with no committee vote and no movement toward the floor.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are long-lasting chemicals used in manufacturing that do not break down and accumulate in water, food, and people's bodies. This bill would require the EPA to set federal water pollution limits on PFAS discharges from eight industries, including chemical and plastics plants, metal finishers, textile mills, and landfills, and to publish official water quality safety criteria for the chemicals. It would also require monitoring at additional dischargers, establish a standard test method for detecting PFAS, and provide $200 million a year for five years to help publicly owned wastewater treatment plants keep PFAS out of the water system.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water drawn from rivers and lakes that receive industrial wastewater, communities near PFAS-emitting plants, and publicly owned wastewater treatment plants and their ratepayers, who currently bear the cost of removing PFAS that industries discharge into their systems.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the EPA to publish final effluent limitations guidelines limiting PFAS discharges for eight industry categories on a fixed schedule: organic chemicals, plastics and synthetic fibers, electroplating, and metal finishing by September 2026; textile mills and landfills by September 2027; and leather tanning, paint formulating, and plastics molding by September 2028.

It requires the EPA to publish human health water quality criteria for PFAS under the Clean Water Act within three years, giving states enforceable benchmarks for how much PFAS may be present in rivers, lakes, and coastal waters.

It authorizes $200 million a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 in grants to publicly owned wastewater treatment plants to carry out pretreatment programs and track down the local sources of PFAS entering their systems, shifting part of the cleanup burden away from ratepayers.

It requires the EPA to formally promulgate Method 1633A, the EPA's validated test for measuring PFAS in water, solids, and tissue samples, by January 2026, so monitoring and enforcement rest on a single reliable standard.

It requires monitoring of PFAS discharges beginning immediately upon enactment for the eight covered industries and for pulp and paper mills, airports, and electrical and electronic components facilities, including discharges sent to public treatment works.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall mainly on PFAS-emitting industries, which would have to measure and limit their discharges, including chemical, plastics, electroplating, metal finishing, and textile companies; those costs could be passed to consumers through higher prices. Taxpayers would fund the EPA work and the treatment-plant grants if Congress appropriates the money.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs could be significant for smaller metal finishing, electroplating, and tanning businesses, and some costs could be passed on to consumers through higher prices for manufactured goods.

The grant program for wastewater treatment plants is subject to the availability of appropriations, so the $200 million a year is only authorized, not guaranteed, and Congress must fund the EPA's rulemaking work separately.

The bill does not ban PFAS manufacture or address drinking water standards directly; it only limits what industries may discharge, and it gives the EPA discretion to decline developing limits for pulp and paper mills, airports, and electronics facilities, provided it explains its reasoning.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a substantial reduction in a class of chemicals that persists in water and accumulates in people's bodies, with the burden of limiting pollution placed on the industries that create it rather than on water customers. The costs are real but ordinary for pollution control: monitoring and treatment expenses for discharging industries, funded appropriations, and possible price effects. The design is fairly targeted, with staged deadlines that give different industries time to comply.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in December 2025 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and in February 2026 it was sent to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, where it awaits any action.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) introduced the bill on December 11, 2025, with Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
On February 2, 2026, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, a routine step from which most bills never advance without their committee chair's support.
The bill has one cosponsor, Rep. Fitzpatrick, and no committee or subcommittee vote has occurred since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, PFAS-emitting industries are better off than they would be under the bill: no federal discharge limits for PFAS have been imposed on them, and the bill has not advanced far enough to change that.

for.name: Brian Fitzpatrick
for.role: U.S. Representative (PA), the bill's only cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two supporters are a Democrat (Pappas of New Hampshire) and a Republican (Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania); no votes have been taken, and no member or group has been recorded opposing it.

industries.industry: Chemical, plastics, and synthetic fibers manufacturers
industries.note: The first industry facing mandatory PFAS discharge limits under the bill, due by September 2026. Limits on their PFAS emissions are the main benefit the bill delivers for water quality.
Covered industries that discharge PFAS into water systems, including through public treatment plants, and would face monitoring and limits within a year of passage.

industries.industry: Textile mills, leather tanners, and paint and plastics formulators
industries.note: Industrial users of PFAS-facing chemicals whose discharges would be monitored immediately and limited by 2027 or 2028 under the bill.
Sources of PFAS runoff that would face monitoring requirements; landfills would also get discharge limits by 2027.

industries.industry: Publicly owned wastewater treatment utilities and their ratepayers
industries.note: These plants receive $200 million a year in authorized grants to intercept PFAS before it enters the system, sparing ratepayers some treatment costs; they are currently stuck treating PFAS that industries discharge to them.
Universal monitoring requirements across many industries would create a large, steady market for PFAS testing using the standardized Method 1633A.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to a subcommittee with only one cosponsor rarely reach the House floor on their own. The realistic paths are that it stalls quietly, attracts more cosponsors if PFAS contamination draws attention in members' districts, or gets folded into a larger water infrastructure bill such as the Water Resources Development Act, where its standards could survive even if the standalone bill does not move.
